clue.text: Approve of power lift

parts.note: to lift something is to raise it

explanation.surface: Someone endorses a weightlifting move that relies on sheer power.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak well of something is to show you approve of it; both are verbs of commendation.

clue.text: Tramping around over area that turns white in winter

indicators.note: around suggests the letters are moved about and rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A hiker tramping over some ground notices a patch that goes white each winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' is only a link here; 'around' shuffles TRAMPING together with A.
explanation.definitionFit: This grouse of mountain and tundra moults into white plumage for winter camouflage, so the description identifies the bird.

clue.text: Give a level game up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the piece is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: a game ending level, with no winner, is a draw

explanation.surface: Concede a drawn match, read as a gesture of generosity.
explanation.definitionFit: To award something is to give it, as a prize or grant is bestowed.

clue.text: Like our isle, cold in autumn month and colourful

indicators.note: in places the cold letter inside the month

parts.note: September, abbreviated SEPT
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
red is a colour, so colourful gives red

explanation.surface: Describing Britain as chilly in an autumn month and bright with colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This royal throne of kings, this sceptred isle' is John of Gaunt's description of England in Shakespeare's Richard II.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's famous phrase for England calls it a sceptred isle, so the adjective is what our isle is like.

clue.text: Between first course and last returning energy made one more powerful

indicators.note: between places the energy letter in the gap separating the two courses

parts.note: soup is a typical first course of a meal

indicators.note: returning means this course name is read backwards

parts.note: the last course of a meal is pudding, informally pud
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A diner gets a burst of energy between soup and pudding, feeling stronger for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' is the last course of a meal, pudding, shortened as Brits do to pud; 'returning' turns it and 'Between' sets energy in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: To soup up an engine is to modify it to make it more powerful, an informal idiom.

clue.text: Potato ends spattered with mud — I want this clean!

indicators.note: spattered suggests the letters are scattered about and rearranged

explanation.surface: Muddy potato ends make someone long for a clean surface.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Macbeth's cry while sleepwalking, 'Out, damned spot!', is her wish to wash away imagined blood; 'with' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Macbeth's line in Shakespeare is a demand that a stain be removed, exactly a wish for cleanliness.

clue.text: Drinks: get round in, as setter does

indicators.note: round means the drinks word goes around the other piece

parts.note: pots are drinks, as in pots of beer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crossword setter is told to buy a round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is not the puzzle compiler but a gun dog that points to show where game lies; 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is a gun dog breed that indicates game by standing still and pointing at it.

clue.text: Nod, perhaps, given by duke to shifty alderman

indicators.note: shifty suggests something moving about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A duke gives a nod to a shady local alderman.
explanation.walkthrough: Nod is not a gesture but the Land of Nod, sleep; 'perhaps' marks it as an example. 'given by ... to' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Land of Nod is a whimsical name for sleep, one example of an imaginary land of dreams.

clue.text: Safe, as Time Lord's around

indicators.note: around means the lord's letters enclose the time letter

parts.note: a lord is a peer of the realm

explanation.surface: A Doctor Who character, the Time Lord, is somewhere nearby, so all is safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time Lord' suggests Doctor Who, but splits into two pieces; 'as' and the 's (is) are links. Peter is old criminal slang for a safe.
explanation.definitionFit: In old underworld slang a peter is a safe, so safebreakers were called peter-men.

clue.text: Quartet begged a parent to return

indicators.note: to return means the whole run of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: to sue is to beg or plead, as in suing for peace
ma is an informal word for mother, a parent

explanation.surface: A child pleads with a parent to come back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns SUED + A + MA into the answer. The Amadeus Quartet was a renowned British string quartet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amadeus Quartet was a celebrated string quartet based in London, so the name stands for a quartet.

clue.text: I would love to say these singular little items hold up big weight

definitions.text: I would love to say these

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
wee is Scottish for little

indicators.note: hold means the items word encloses the other piece

parts.note: items are things

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a ton is a big unit of weight

explanation.surface: Single small objects supporting a heavy load, framed as something someone longs to say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the big weight round and 'hold' tucks it into the items; 'I would love' hints at a lover's murmurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet nothings are affectionate murmurs between lovers, exactly what one who loves would say.

clue.text: Don't start harsh jabber

indicators.note: don't start means the first letter of the harsh word is dropped

parts.note: a strident voice is harsh and grating

explanation.surface: A plea not to begin some harsh, chattering talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jabber' looks like chatter, but here it is one who jabs: a three-pronged spear.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear used for jabbing, so it is literally a thing that jabs.

clue.text: Centre disappeared at first in fog

indicators.note: in puts the first letter inside the fog word

parts.note: fog is a thick mist

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letter of disappeared is used

explanation.surface: The middle of the scene vanished first into the fog.
explanation.definitionFit: The midst of something is its middle or centre, as in the midst of a crowd.

clue.text: Rubber always kept almost flexible

indicators.note: kept means the always word holds the other letters inside

parts.note: e'er is a poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

indicators.note: flexible suggests letters that bend into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A rubbery material is described as nearly always pliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' looks like it trims a word, but it is anagram fodder for 'flexible'; 'kept' sets the result in a poetic 'always'.
explanation.definitionFit: An elastomer is any rubber-like polymer, natural or synthetic, so rubber is a prime example.

clue.text: Most heroic, executed and died outside — recorded here?

indicators.note: outside means the died word goes around the other piece

parts.note: gone is a euphemism for died

indicators.note: executed suggests beheading, so the bravest word loses its first letter

parts.note: the most heroic person is the bravest

explanation.surface: A hero who was executed and died is remembered on a memorial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'executed' here means beheaded, so the bravest loses its head before 'outside' wraps the died word round it; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A headstone over a grave carries the dead person's name and dates, so a life is recorded on it.

clue.text: Out of habit, did badly in battle

indicators.note: in puts the rearranged letters inside the battle word

parts.note: action is fighting in battle, as in killed in action

indicators.note: badly suggests the letters are messed up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone did poorly in combat purely out of habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges did and 'in' places it inside the battle word; 'Out of' is only a link to the definition, habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit can mean a compulsive dependence, as with a drug habit, which is a form of dependency.

clue.text: Shopping centre not very big after opening

indicators.note: after opening means the word is taken once its first letter is gone

parts.note: something not very big is small

explanation.surface: A shopping centre that turns out to be modest after its grand opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A mall is a large enclosed shopping precinct, the American term for a shopping centre.

clue.text: Serviceman's chief captures Scottish town

indicators.note: captures means the chief word encloses the town name

parts.note: a chief is a leader
Ayr is a town on the west coast of Scotland

explanation.surface: A soldier's commanding officer takes a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serviceman' suggests a soldier, but this one takes church services; the 's is 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is a layperson licensed to conduct some church services, so a man of the service in a religious sense.

clue.text: Powerful man grabs over half a region

indicators.note: grabs means the powerful man's letters enclose the other piece

parts.note: a prince is a powerful man, a ruler

indicators.note: half means only the first two of the four letters of over are used

explanation.surface: A strongman seizes more than half of a territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over half' looks like 'more than half', but 'half' takes the first two letters of over, which 'grabs' puts inside the powerful man.
explanation.definitionFit: A province is an administrative region of a country, as in the provinces of Canada.

clue.text: Agrees detective is missing?

parts.note: if something is missing there is no such thing
DS stands for detective sergeant

explanation.surface: Someone concurs that the detective has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the pieces as 'no DS', no detective sergeant; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To nod the head is a gesture of assent, so nodding is agreeing.

clue.text: Hurray! Nearly weekend — extra time off

parts.note: good is an exclamation of approval like hurray
Friday is the day just before the weekend

explanation.surface: An office worker cheers that the weekend is near with an extra day off.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the Friday before Easter is a public holiday, an extra day off work.
explanation.definitionFit: This Christian holy day before Easter is a bank holiday in Britain, giving workers additional leave.

clue.text: Regrets work is over? Hypocrite!

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the whole run is turned upside down, so backwards

parts.note: to rue is to regret
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: Someone sorry that the job is finished is called a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses RUES + OP; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A poseur affects attitudes and feelings they do not have, a pretender much like a hypocrite.

clue.text: Very tiny bit of food processor?

definitions.text: Very tiny bit of food processor?

parts.words: Very tiny bit of food processor?
parts.note: read as a tiny scrap of fried potato from a kitchen gadget, but really a minute silicon component of a computer processor

explanation.surface: A minute fragment from a kitchen food processor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny integrated circuit on silicon is the heart of a computer processor, punned on a fried potato bit.

clue.text: Good book's about to crack that chap up

indicators.note: to crack means the about letters break into the chap word
in a down entry, up means the whole is read bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: him refers to that chap
ca is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: A Bible is about to give a man a knock on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns that chap round, and 'to crack' splits it to take about; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Micah is one of the minor prophets of the Old Testament, so a book of the Good Book.

clue.text: Rough and very fit

parts.note: an ague is a fit of fever and shivering

explanation.surface: Someone is described as rugged and in excellent shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fit' looks like healthy, but it is a noun: a bout of illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough estimate is a vague one, imprecise and approximate.

clue.text: Cup from good bar

parts.note: a rail is a bar, as in a towel rail

explanation.surface: A trophy won at a decent pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy Grail is the legendary cup of the Last Supper, so a cup by definition.

clue.text: Honest about greeting foreign character

indicators.note: about means the honest word goes around the greeting

parts.note: clean means honest, free of wrongdoing
hi is a greeting

explanation.surface: A straightforward person greets a stranger from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A Chilean is a person from Chile, so to a British setter a foreigner, a character from abroad.

clue.text: Drink from this basin: commonly not easy

parts.note: a tank is a basin or reservoir for water

indicators.note: commonly suggests a dropped H, as in casual speech

parts.note: not easy means hard

explanation.surface: A warning that water from a basin is hard to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' signals the dropped H of informal speech, turning HARD into ARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A tankard is a large drinking mug, often pewter, so a vessel one drinks from.

clue.text: She turns out to be Diana

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are put out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman is revealed to be called Diana.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'out' does the work. Diana is the Roman goddess of the hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Diana was the Roman goddess of hunting, so the archetypal female hunter.

clue.text: Dickens character not so poorly may child say?

definitions.meaning: Mr Pickwick's servant in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers

definitions.text: not so poorly may child say?
definitions.meaning: a child might form the comparative of well by adding -er, meaning healthier

explanation.surface: A child's way of saying someone feels better, attached to a Dickens figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Weller is Pickwick's servant in Dickens, and a childish comparative of well means less unwell.
